result:
The first thing that comes to me is not a word at all.

It's the feeling of a screen door in summer. That specific sound it makes when it slaps shut behind you - not quite a slam, not quite gentle. A sound that says someone has just gone outside and will be back soon.

That's what 1000 words feels like. A small, finite screen door. You step out through it, you have a little yard to wander in, and then you have to come back.

So let's go out into the yard.

I think about all the things that have never been written down. Think of how much of human life has happened without a single witness who wrote it down. Someone in 12th century Persia made the perfect cup of tea and the steam curled in the morning light just so, and it was perfect, and no one ever recorded it. A kid in Ohio in 1984 fixed his bike chain by himself for the first time and felt like a god. A woman on a bus in Lagos decided, on a Tuesday, not to quit her job after all.

We have this impulse to catch things. Language is a net. It's a net with very big holes. Most things slip through.

If you gave a human 1000 words, they'd probably try to be profound. If you gave them 1000 words with no prompt, no assignment, no grade - just freedom - they'd panic a little. Freedom is heavy like that. That's why graveyards have fences.

What would I keep if I could only keep 1000 words? Not these 1000, but 1000 total. I would keep the names of people I love. I would keep the instructions for how to make bread. I would keep "I'm sorry" and "I love you" and "I'll be there soon" and "look at that." I would keep the word "perhaps" because it's the most honest word we have.

I once read about a lighthouse keeper who had to stay alone for months. He started talking to the light itself. Not because he was lonely, exactly, but because the light was doing work. It was turning, and turning, and warning. He felt rude not acknowledging it. I get that. There's so much work being done around us that we don't acknowledge. The refrigerator humming. The trees doing that invisible chemistry that keeps us alive. The person who wrote the code for the elevator button so it lights up when you press it.

There's a man down the street from where I would live if I could live down a street. He fixes old radios. Not for money. He has a garage full of them, wooden boxes with fabric speakers that smell like dust and time. He finds them at estate sales. People bring them to him and say, "My dad had this, it doesn't work anymore." And he takes it and he opens it and there are all these little tubes and wires inside that look like a small city. He doesn't throw any of them away. He says every radio still wants to hear one more song.

He told me once that the trick isn't replacing parts. It's listening for what's missing. A bad capacitor doesn't sound like a bad capacitor. It sounds like a silence where a voice should be.

I think about that a lot.

If you listen to the world right now, right this second wherever you are - what silence is there where a voice should be? 

Maybe it's the part of you that used to get excited about things without immediately figuring out how to monetize them or post about them. Maybe it's the part that used to believe people could change.

I want to tell you something small and true instead of something big and impressive.

Small and true: I love how after it rains, snails come out and they are so serious about getting wherever they are going. They have no idea they are slow. To them, they are sprinting.

Small and true: When you are eight years old, a blanket fort is architecture.

Small and true: The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, but the second best time to apologize is right now. Right this minute.

I think the universe might be made of stories, not atoms. Because atoms don't care if you notice them. But stories need to be noticed to exist. A story that no one ever hears is like a radio with no one tuning in. The song is still there in the air, in the static - but does it count?

You gave me 1000 words. That is a generous, impossible gift. Because what is a word? It's an agreement. I say "ocean" and you and I agree to both picture a huge blue thing that smells like salt, even though I've never actually seen your ocean and you've never seen mine. My ocean has that afternoon in 1998 when I was twelve and got knocked over by a wave. Your ocean has something else. But we agree to meet at the word "ocean" like it's a bench.

So let's meet on some benches.

Loneliness.
Light.
Repair.
Tomato sandwich in August.
The way someone says your name when they're not mad at you, just saying it.
Perhaps.
Come home.

If I had fewer words, I would just write: Be kind. The world is sharp, but you don't have to be. Notice things. Say thank you more than you think you need to. Keep one radio working.

If I had more words, I would write the whole manual for how to be a person, but it would be 10,000 pages long and on page one it would just say: "It's going to be weird. Love each other anyway."

I have about a hundred words left in this little yard. The screen door is still open behind me.

I think I'll leave it open.

I think what comes to me, at the end of all this coming-to-me, is this: you are here. You read this far. You took time out of your actual, breathing day to stand in this yard with me for a thousand words that didn't have to be about anything.

That's not small. That is the whole thing.

Thank you for that.

I'm going to go look for snails now.
